mainEntity.name: Is being edentulous the same as being toothless?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in clinical terms, edentulous is the professional dental descriptor for being without natural teeth. Completely edentulous means all natural teeth are absent, while partially edentulous refers to having lost some but not all teeth. The term is used by dental professionals to categorise a patient's dental status and help plan appropriate restorative treatment. If your dentist has used this term during a consultation, it simply means they are describing the current state of your dentition in clinical language.

mainEntity.name: Can dental implants always replace missing teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implants may be a suitable option for many patients, but they are not universally appropriate. Suitability depends on the amount and quality of available jawbone, general health, gum health, and lifestyle factors such as smoking. A detailed clinical and radiographic assessment — including X-rays or cone beam CT scanning — is required to evaluate whether implants are feasible for a particular patient. In some cases, preparatory treatment such as bone grafting may be required before implant placement can proceed.

mainEntity.name: What happens to the jawbone after tooth loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: When a tooth is lost, the jawbone in that area no longer receives the stimulation it previously received through chewing forces transmitted via the tooth root. As a result, the bone begins to resorb — gradually reducing in height and width over time. This process can progress for months or years and may affect the fit of dentures, the appearance of the face, and the feasibility of future implant placement. This is one reason why addressing tooth loss sooner rather than later is generally advisable from a clinical perspective.

mainEntity.name: Are there alternatives to dental implants for edentulous patients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Dental implants are one of several restorative options. Conventional removable dentures — full or partial — remain a commonly used and clinically appropriate solution for many patients. Fixed dental bridges, which attach to adjacent natural teeth, may also be considered for partially edentulous patients where suitable abutment teeth are available. The most appropriate option for any individual patient will depend on their clinical circumstances, general health, preferences, and dental history, and should always be determined through professional consultation.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to get dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: The dental implant process typically takes several months from initial assessment to completion of the final restoration. This is because osseointegration — the process by which the titanium implant fuses with the surrounding bone — requires healing time, usually between eight and sixteen weeks, though this varies between individuals. Additional time may be required if preparatory procedures such as bone grafting are necessary. Your dental team will provide a personalised treatment timeline during the planning phase of your care.

mainEntity.name: Can gum disease be treated before considering implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. In fact, addressing any active gum disease before implant treatment is generally considered an important part of responsible treatment planning. Peri-implantitis — a condition affecting the tissues around an implant — shares risk factors with periodontal disease, and implants placed in the presence of uncontrolled gum disease are at higher risk of failure. Your dental team will assess and, where needed, treat periodontal conditions before discussing implant candidacy. This staged approach is consistent with good clinical practice.
